# Scope of This Session {background-color="#530153"}

# Recap and Introduction {background-color="#530153"}

## Recap

- AI is a skilled but naive RA requiring guidance.
- Agents search files for prompt-relevant guidance to add to the context window.
- Use memory files for project-specific content you always want AI to find or that cannot be found in your files.
- Cramming every use case into the memory file makes it dominate the context window.
- Irrelevant information competes for and distracts the AI's attention from the specific prompt.

## Progressive Disclosure

- Instructions can be loaded only when the agent deems them relevant.
- This is called **progressive disclosure**. It is central to skills, but not unique to them.
- In the last session, we used progressive disclosure to point to codebooks from the memory file.

```markdown
### Input Datasets
- data/raw/census_2011.csv - Household demographics. Main variables: household ID,
  income. When needed, full codebook: data/raw/census_2011_codebook.csv
```

# Skills: Purpose {background-color="#530153"}

## Memory Files vs. Skills

| | Memory files | Skills |
|---|---|---|
| Typical purpose | Domain knowledge and instructions relevant for every prompt | Detailed instructions relevant only for specific prompt use cases |
| Added to every new context window? | Yes | No, only when the agent thinks they are needed |
| Need to be token-efficient? | Yes, because they are always loaded | Much less so, because they are loaded only when relevant |
| Project-specific or domain-specific? | Mostly project-specific; reuse but adapt common sections | Domain-specific, including tools, research fields, econometrics, and personal preferences; reusable across projects |

## Efficient Way to Provide Details

- All available skill descriptions are loaded into each new context window.
- Only when a skill is relevant is the full content loaded.
- Therefore, skills can contain details such as:
  - Step-by-step instructions for a task
  - What the agent should ask or confirm before proceeding
  - Templates for the expected output format

# Skills: Format {background-color="#530153"}

## Skills Format

- Skills are files with natural-language content, similar to memory files.
- A skill requires frontmatter with at least a name and a description.
- The description is not what the skill does. It tells the agent when to use it and when not to use it.

```markdown
---
name: new-shiny-dash
description: Use when setting up a new dashboard - use when Shiny or no specific
  dashboard tool is specified
---
# New Shiny Dashboard Skill
Always start from the templates in `templates/` and build toward one of the
`examples/`. If not sure which example is the best fit, ask the user.
Then populate it by [...]
```

## Open-Source Folder Format

- Minimum requirement: a `SKILL.md` file in a folder named after the skill.
- The skill folder may contain resources in subfolders referenced by the skill file.
- The skill is everything in the skill folder; resources are used through progressive disclosure.

```text
skills/
|-- stata-skill/
|   `-- SKILL.md              Instructions for the Stata skill
`-- new-shiny-dash/
    |-- SKILL.md              Instructions for the skill
    |-- templates/             Files for the agent to start from
    `-- examples/              Examples of end results
```

## Skills Folder Location

- The skill folder has a standardized format, but where to save it differs by agent.
- Similar to memory files, agents will eventually find and use skills even when the location is not their native one.

| Skill folder location | Agent | Cross-agent compatibility |
|---|---|---|
| `.agents/skills/` | Open-source format, such as Cursor and Codex | Commonly used as a backup by other agents |
| `.claude/skills/` | Claude | Well-recognized and quickly found by most agents |
| `.github/skills/` | GitHub Copilot | Less well-recognized, but eventually found and used |

# Skills: Installation {background-color="#530153"}

## Installation

- Many skills are not project-specific. Install skills written by others.
- More skills do not automatically mean a better agent. Agents are nudged to use skills over generic knowledge.
- Sometimes you want general knowledge. Too many skills can make the agent find a skill when it is not needed.
- Do not worry about adding a few more skills; the point is not to install the whole universe of skills.

## Manual Installation

- A skill folder only needs to be saved in your project.
- Manual installation works anywhere, regardless of how the skill was published.
- Knowing how to install manually helps with troubleshooting.

### How to Install

1. Locate or create your skills folder.
2. Download or copy the full skill folder, including all its content, into your skills folder.
3. Type `/skills` in the Agent and confirm that your skill is there.

## Demo: Manual Installation

## Installation Tools

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Command line

- Requires basic knowledge of command-line tools.
- Install Node.js using the installation guide or eServices Software Installation.
- Follow the Skills documentation at <https://skills.sh/docs>.
- This is emerging as an industry standard, so use it if the CLI is not intimidating.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### VS Code extension

- Essentially a wrapper for the CLI tool.
- Requires no CLI knowledge.
- No extension has yet been published by a well-established trusted source.
- Once VS Code or another trusted source releases an extension with many downloads, use this approach.
:::

::::

Manual installation is always available. Use it until a tool you trust becomes available.

# Skills: Library and Examples {background-color="#530153"}

## Skills Library

- We are still populating the library at <https://github.com/dime-worldbank/coding-agents-hub>.
- As with memory files, this is where we want to share skill examples for different purposes.
- Share skills that you have used and found useful.

## Example Skill: Stata

- Stata usage is much smaller than R and especially Python, so Stata is less represented in an agent's generic knowledge.
- Adding a Stata skill to a project with Stata code can make a big difference.
- Example: <https://github.com/dylantmoore/stata-skill>

## Example Skill: Literature Review

Example: <https://meleantonio.github.io/awesome-econ-ai-stuff/skills/literature/lit-review-assistant/index>

```markdown
---
name: lit-review-assistant
description: Search, summarize, and synthesize economics literature
---
[...]
## Instructions
### Step 1: Define the Research Domain
Ask the user:
1. What is your specific research question?
2. What's the scope? (Narrow field survey vs. cross-disciplinary review)
3. What databases do you have access to? (JSTOR, EconLit, Google Scholar, NBER)
4. What time period is relevant?
5. Are there seminal papers to start from?
[...]
```

## mAI Skills

- mAI is not a code agent with access to your code files, so the use case is different, but it is a great place to experiment.
- Go to <https://ai.worldbank.org/mai/skills/> and use the **Create Skill** wizard.
